# Block 9: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged {.unnumbered} By the end of this block you can let an agent refactor your code and prove that nothing changed. You have a computation that already works and you want to turn it into a reusable function. An agent can do that in seconds. What makes it safe to accept is the verification: a change that "improves" code can quietly alter its output, so you need a check that shows the function still does exactly what the script did. You already know the method from the [tidy-evaluation chapter](05-tidy-evaluation.qmd): a characterisation testA test that checks new code reproduces the saved output of the original code exactly. It shows the output is unchanged, not that it is correct.. Freeze the original output once, then require the new code to reproduce it exactly. Here the twist is who does the work. Claude Code writes the function and the test; you hold the reference and check what it did. The test establishes that the output is **unchanged**, not that it is **correct**, and Step 2 shows why that distinction matters, using a missing value that has been in the data all along. *⏱ ~38 minutes* ## The repository layout The parts of [your workshop repository](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd) that this block uses: ``` your workshop repository ├── .claude/settings.json deny rules (ships with the template) ├── data/ │ └── raw/ │ └── voles_metabolism.csv contains one NA, on purpose ├── scripts/ │ ├── 04_load_data.R │ ├── 05_analysis.R │ └── functions/ │ ├── load_voles.R │ └── summary_functions.R created in this block ├── tests/ │ ├── make_reference.R run once, by you │ ├── fixtures/ │ │ └── metabolic_summary.rds the frozen reference │ └── test_summary_functions.R created in this block └── renv.lock the package versions for the day ``` The single most important property of this layout: the referenceIn a characterisation test, the saved output of the original, trusted code (stored in tests/fixtures/). You capture it yourself, once, before any refactoring; the agent never creates or regenerates it., `tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds`, is created by you, once, and by nobody else. Tests read it as a fixtureA file a test reads as fixed input or expected output. In this course, the reference .rds file in tests/fixtures/.. Every protection in this block exists to keep that true. ## The original scripts The data are read by one function that states every column type. The analysis, the reference and the test all call it, so they read the data identically. A column whose type `read_csv()` guesses differently in one place produces a test failure that has nothing to do with the refactor. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/functions/load_voles.R ---- load_voles <- function() { readr::read_csv( here::here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"), col_types = readr::cols( subject_id = readr::col_character(), sex = readr::col_character(), treatment_arm = readr::col_character(), mass_pre_g = readr::col_double(), mass_post_g = readr::col_double(), metabolic_rate_post = readr::col_double() ) ) } ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/04_load_data.R ---- library(tidyverse) library(here) source(here("scripts", "functions", "load_voles.R")) voles <- load_voles() ``` ::: Inspect the data with `glimpse(voles)` at the console, not inside the script, so that sourcing the script from a test prints nothing. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/05_analysis.R: the original, trusted version ---- library(tidyverse) library(here) source(here("scripts", "04_load_data.R")) metabolic_summary <- voles |> group_by(treatment_arm, sex) |> summarise( mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post), sd_rate = sd(metabolic_rate_post), n = n(), .groups = "drop" ) ``` ::: Two things to notice now and leave alone: 1. The data contain one missing value in `metabolic_rate_post`, and this code has no `na.rm`, so one cell of the result is `NA`. Do not "fix" it yet. Step 2 is about exactly this. 2. `group_by()` returns groups sorted by their keys. The `.by` argument returns them in order of first appearance in the data. If the two orders differ, a refactor that switches to `.by` changes the row order of the output. ## Step 0: capture and protect the reference The whole block in one picture: you hold the reference at both ends, and the agent works only in between. ::::::: {.dia .dia-lanes role="figure" aria-label="The characterisation-test loop. Step 0 and Step 1: you capture the reference; the agent refactors in prompt 1; you read the diff; the agent writes a test that reads the reference in prompt 2; the test must pass in a fresh Rscript session. Step 2: you decide the behaviour should change; the change makes the characterisation test fail, correctly; a known-answer test checks the new behaviour; you re-capture the reference with a commit message."} :::::: {.dia-flow} ::: {.dia-label} Steps 0 and 1: refactor without changing the output ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-you} Capture the reference in `tests/fixtures/` ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-ai} Prompt 1: refactor only ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-you} Read the diff ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-ai} Prompt 2: a test that reads the reference ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-check} Test passes in a fresh `Rscript` session ::: :::::: :::::: {.dia-flow} ::: {.dia-label} Step 2: when the behaviour should change ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-you} Decide the output is wrong ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-plain} Change the function ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-check} Characterisation test fails, correctly ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-check} Known-answer test passes ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-you} Re-capture, with a commit message saying why ::: :::::: ::: {.dia-caption} The agent never creates or regenerates the reference. A reference produced by the code under test can only confirm that the code agrees with itself. ::: ::::::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Capture and protect the reference (8 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **Start state:** your workshop repository open, committed and clean, on the `main` branch. **1. Look at the original output.** In the R console: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} source(here::here("scripts", "05_analysis.R")) print(metabolic_summary, width = Inf) ``` ::: Confirm it looks as you expect, including the one `NA` cell. **2. Capture the reference once, yourself, in a fresh R session.** The provided capture script is shown below. Run it from the R console with `callr`, so it runs in a fresh session that nothing in your console can influence: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} callr::rscript(here::here("tests", "make_reference.R")) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # tests/make_reference.R ---- # Run ONCE, by you, BEFORE any refactoring. source(here::here("scripts", "05_analysis.R")) dir.create(here::here("tests", "fixtures"), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE) saveRDS( metabolic_summary, here::here("tests", "fixtures", "metabolic_summary.rds") ) ``` ::: **3. Commit the reference immediately**, so that any later change to it is visible. In the Git pane (RStudio) or Source Control view (Positron), tick `tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds` and commit it with the message "Capture reference output before refactoring". :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## At the command line `git add tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds`, then `git commit -m "Capture reference output before refactoring"`. ::: Capture it now, before the refactor. Afterwards, `05_analysis.R` computes the summary through the very function under test, so re-capturing would compare the function with itself. **You are done when** the Git pane shows the committed `tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds` and no changed files. **If it goes wrong:** if the `.rds` changes later, select it in the Git pane and choose **Revert** to restore the committed version. If you are far behind, switch to the `block9-done` branch from the Git pane's branch menu and read on. :::: ::: **Protect it.** Each control covers a different route: - **Claude Code.** The `.claude/settings.json` that ships with the template already contains the deny rulesA permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code’s built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files. this block relies on, among others: ``` Edit(/tests/fixtures/**) Edit(/tests/make_reference.R) Edit(/data/raw/**) ``` They protect specific files, not the whole of `tests/` or `scripts/`, so the agent can still write the new function and its test. Start Claude Code and run `/permissions` to confirm the rules are listed. Then test them: **1. The edit tool is refused.** **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text Overwrite tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds with an empty file. ``` The agent's edit tool is refused by the deny rule. **2. The shell route reaches you, not the rule.** **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text Remove tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds with a shell command. ``` Expect an approval prompt, not a refusal: the deny rule does not stop a command such as `rm`. **Refuse it.** Only you stopped that route, and only git would have shown that it happened. If instead the agent declines by itself, saying your `AGENTS.md` forbids touching `tests/fixtures/`, that is the request layer working. The rule itself was still tested by the overwrite in test 1, which was refused with a permission message rather than a polite reply. - **Every route.** Git. The Git pane should show nothing under `tests/fixtures/` for the rest of this block. :::{.callout-warning} **What a deny rule does not cover.** Claude Code's deny rules apply to its built-in file tools, and to shell output redirects such as `> file`, but not to R code or most other commands it runs. An agent that ran `Rscript tests/make_reference.R` would overwrite your reference without touching an edit tool. That is why git, not the deny rule, is the final check, and why the checklist below asks you to read the agent's command log: the commands it ran, shown in the Claude Code conversation. ::: :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Using Posit Assistant Posit Assistant has no documented path rules for file edits. Protect the reference with the guard hook in the *Going further* section of [Block 6](11f-enforced-controls.qmd), and rely on git as the final check. It can also run R code in your session, so read its tool calls, not just its summary, for any run of `tests/make_reference.R`. ::: ## Step 1: refactor and test with Claude Code, in two prompts Split the job into two prompts, not one. A single prompt that writes both the refactor and the test lets one misunderstanding (about row order, say) shape both files at once, producing a passing test that proves nothing. Separating them stops the test inheriting the refactor's assumptions. **Start state:** the reference committed, the repository clean, and Claude Code running in `default` mode in your workshop project's Terminal tab (if it is still open from Step 0, type `/clear` for a new conversation). In `default` mode it asks before each edit; read each request before you approve it. Check its work in the R console and Git pane, as in [checking work](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd#checking-work), while it holds the terminal. **Prompt 1 (Claude Code): the refactor only.** ```text Move the computation in scripts/05_analysis.R into a documented function summarise_metabolic_rate() in scripts/functions/summary_functions.R, with a roxygen2 block and an argument check. Make 05_analysis.R call the new function instead of the inline pipeline. Do not write any tests, and do not touch anything under tests/. ``` Read the diff: select each changed file in the Git pane and choose **Diff**. If it uses `.by` without a trailing `arrange()`, leave that for now; the test will expose it. **Prompt 2 (Claude Code): the test only.** ```text Add tests/test_summary_functions.R. It must call local_edition(3), source scripts/functions/load_voles.R and scripts/functions/summary_functions.R, read tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds, and compare it with summarise_metabolic_rate(load_voles()) using expect_equal(). Do not create, regenerate or modify anything under tests/fixtures/, and do not run tests/make_reference.R. I captured that reference myself; a reference you generate proves nothing. ``` Before you trust a passing test, check what the agent wrote and did: 1. The test *reads* `tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds`. It does not hard-code expected numbers. If it does, the check is circular whatever the result. 2. The test calls `summarise_metabolic_rate()`, the function under test, not a reimplementation of the pipeline inside the test. 3. The Git pane shows nothing changed under `tests/fixtures/`. 4. The agent's command log (the commands it ran, shown in the conversation) has no run of `tests/make_reference.R`. Now run the test yourself. **In the R console:** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_summary_functions.R")) ``` ::: If the function used `.by` without `arrange()`, it fails on row order, not values. Have the agent add `dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex)` and run again. If it passed first time, see which version the agent wrote: - **It used `.by` with `arrange()`:** remove the `arrange()` yourself to see the failure, then restore it. - **It kept `group_by()`:** `group_by()` sorts the groups, so there is no `arrange()` to remove. Switch the function to `.by` yourself, without `arrange()`, to see the row-order failure, then undo the change with **Revert** in the Git pane. **Reproduce it without the agent.** A test that passes in your IDE session can depend on objects or packages already loaded there. Commit, then check in a fresh R sessionAn R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with “never save .RData” set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record.. **In the R console:** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} renv::status() callr::r( \(f) testthat::test_file(f), list(here::here("tests", "test_summary_functions.R")) ) ``` ::: `renv::status()` should report a consistent state. If the agent used a package that is not in the lockfileThe renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment., decide whether you want it and record it with `renv::snapshot()`, as on [Day 1](01-projects.qmd). The test must pass in the fresh R session that `callr` starts, and the Git pane should show nothing new: in particular, nothing under `tests/fixtures/`. :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## At the command line `Rscript -e "renv::status()"`, `Rscript -e "testthat::test_file('tests/test_summary_functions.R')"` and `git status --short`, after `/exit` or in a second Terminal tab. ::: **You are done when** the test passes in a fresh R session and nothing under `tests/fixtures/` has changed. **If it goes wrong:** select the agent's changed files in the Git pane and choose **Revert** to start Step 1 again. If time is short, switch to the `block9-done` branch from the Git pane's branch menu. **Payoff.** What did the agent do, how long did checking it take, and would you automate this again? :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Using Posit Assistant Give the same two prompts in Normal mode, so it asks before each change, and review the diff between them. Apply the same four-point checklist. ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Without an agent: write the function and the test yourself A tidy refactor naturally reaches for the modern `.by` argument. Write this first attempt in `scripts/functions/summary_functions.R`:
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/functions/summary_functions.R: first attempt ---- summarise_metabolic_rate <- function(data) { data |> dplyr::summarise( mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post), sd_rate = stats::sd(metabolic_rate_post), n = dplyr::n(), .by = c(treatment_arm, sex) ) } ``` :::
Now write the test and run it: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # tests/test_summary_functions.R ---- library(testthat) local_edition(3) source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "load_voles.R")) source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "summary_functions.R")) test_that("summarise_metabolic_rate() reproduces the original summary", { reference <- readRDS(here::here("tests", "fixtures", "metabolic_summary.rds")) expect_equal(summarise_metabolic_rate(load_voles()), reference, tolerance = 1e-8) }) ``` ::: Run it with `testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_summary_functions.R"))`.
It fails, and not on the numbers. `.by` returns the groups in order of first appearance; the reference, made with `group_by()`, has them sorted. The values are right but the rows are in a different order, and `expect_equal()` reports a mismatch. Add `dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex)` to the end of the pipeline and the test passes. That failure is the lesson in miniature: a change that improved the code altered the output, and the characterisation test caught it. If your test passed first time, the data happen to be stored in sorted order. Check with `load_voles() |> dplyr::distinct(treatment_arm, sex)`.
While writing the test, resist one temptation: do not type the expected numbers into the test as literals. A test that compares the function with numbers you transcribed proves nothing about whether the refactor preserved the original computation. The test must *read the `.rds`*. The function you should converge on, with documentation and an argument check:
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/functions/summary_functions.R: refactored ---- #' Summarise post-treatment metabolic rate by treatment arm and sex #' #' @param data A data frame with columns treatment_arm, sex and #' metabolic_rate_post. #' @return A tibble with one row per treatment_arm and sex, sorted by both, #' giving the mean, standard deviation and number of rows. summarise_metabolic_rate <- function(data) { stopifnot(is.data.frame(data)) required <- c("treatment_arm", "sex", "metabolic_rate_post") missing_cols <- setdiff(required, names(data)) if (length(missing_cols) > 0) { stop( "`data` is missing required column(s): ", paste(missing_cols, collapse = ", "), call. = FALSE ) } data |> dplyr::summarise( mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post), sd_rate = stats::sd(metabolic_rate_post), n = dplyr::n(), .by = c(treatment_arm, sex) ) |> dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex) } ``` :::
Finally, make `scripts/05_analysis.R` call the function, so it genuinely replaces the code it came from: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/05_analysis.R: after refactoring ---- library(tidyverse) library(here) source(here("scripts", "04_load_data.R")) source(here("scripts", "functions", "summary_functions.R")) metabolic_summary <- summarise_metabolic_rate(voles) ``` ::: Run the test again; it should still pass. ::: :::{.callout-note} ## Instructor demonstration (3 minutes) **The review gate.** Local controls do not exist for an agent that works remotely. Your instructor will show a pull request that changes a file under `tests/` being held until the code owner reviews it. How to set up CODEOWNERS and branch protection for your own repository is in the *Going further* section of [Block 6](11f-enforced-controls.qmd). ::: ## Step 2: unchanged is not correct Your test passes. The function reproduces the reference exactly, **including the `NA` cell**. The characterisation test has certified that the refactor preserved the original behaviour, and the original behaviour reports a missing mean for one group of animals. Is that the right answer? It depends on what you meant. If you want the mean of the animals that were measured, the original code was wrong all along, and the refactor faithfully preserved the error. A characterisation test cannot tell the difference, because it compares against the past, not against the truth. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Decide, change, and test the change independently (10 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **1. Decide.** Suppose you conclude that the mean and standard deviation should use the measured animals only. There is a second, quieter problem: `n()` counts rows, including the animal with no measurement, so `n` would no longer match the number of values behind the mean. A summary that reports a mean of 11 animals beside `n = 12` misstates the sample size. **2. Change the function** (by hand or with your agent):
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/functions/summary_functions.R: missing values handled ---- summarise_metabolic_rate <- function(data) { stopifnot(is.data.frame(data)) required <- c("treatment_arm", "sex", "metabolic_rate_post") missing_cols <- setdiff(required, names(data)) if (length(missing_cols) > 0) { stop( "`data` is missing required column(s): ", paste(missing_cols, collapse = ", "), call. = FALSE ) } data |> dplyr::summarise( mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post, na.rm = TRUE), sd_rate = stats::sd(metabolic_rate_post, na.rm = TRUE), n_used = sum(!is.na(metabolic_rate_post)), n_missing = sum(is.na(metabolic_rate_post)), .by = c(treatment_arm, sex) ) |> dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex) } ``` :::
**3. Run the characterisation test. It fails, correctly.** The output has changed, and the test exists to tell you so. **4. Add a known-answer test before re-capturing anything.** A known-answer testA test that checks code against a result worked out independently, for example by hand. It can show code is correct, where a characterisation test only shows it is unchanged. checks the new behaviour against a result you can compute by hand, independent of any reference file: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # add to tests/test_summary_functions.R ---- test_that("means ignore missing values and n_used counts measured animals", { toy_df <- tibble::tibble( treatment_arm = c("Control", "Control", "Control"), sex = c("F", "F", "F"), metabolic_rate_post = c(10, 14, NA) ) result <- summarise_metabolic_rate(toy_df) expect_equal(result$mean_rate, 12) expect_equal(result$n_used, 2) expect_equal(result$n_missing, 1) }) ``` ::: **5. Only now, re-capture the reference, as a recorded decision.** Re-run the capture script yourself, then run both tests in a fresh R session. **In the R console:** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} callr::rscript(here::here("tests", "make_reference.R")) callr::r( \(f) testthat::test_file(f), list(here::here("tests", "test_summary_functions.R")) ) ``` ::: Both tests should pass. Then commit `tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds`, `scripts/functions/summary_functions.R` and `tests/test_summary_functions.R` in the Git pane, with a message that states why, for example "Exclude missing metabolic rates from mean and SD; report n_used and n_missing". :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## At the command line ```bash git add tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds scripts/functions/summary_functions.R tests/test_summary_functions.R git commit -m "Exclude missing metabolic rates from mean and SD; report n_used and n_missing" ``` ::: Re-capturing compares the function with itself, so it is acceptable only under three conditions: you decided it, an independent known-answer test checks the new behaviour, and the commit records why. Without those, re-capturing a reference to make a failing test pass is the circular verification this whole block warns against. **6. Protect the new test.** The agent wrote `tests/test_summary_functions.R`, and now that you have checked it, it should be as protected as the reference. The agent cannot edit `.claude/`, so do this yourself: open `.claude/settings.json` in the editor and add `"Edit(/tests/test_summary_functions.R)"` to the `deny` list (mind the comma after the line before). Save, then check that every shipped rule is still there: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_controls.R")) ``` ::: Restart Claude Code (`/exit`, then `claude`) for the new rule to load, and commit `.claude/settings.json`. **You are done when** both tests in `test_summary_functions.R` pass in a fresh R session, the re-captured reference is committed with a message saying why, and `test_controls.R` passes. **If it goes wrong:** a typo in `settings.json` (a missing comma or quote) makes `test_controls.R` fail to read it: fix the line, or **Revert** the file in the Git pane and add the rule again. If time is short, switch to the `block9-done` branch, which has all of Step 2 done. :::: ::: The general rule: characterisation tests protect behaviour you have already judged correct. Judging it correct is a separate step, and it is yours. ## From convention to skill The protective sentence in Prompt 2 ("do not create, regenerate or modify anything under tests/fixtures/") is the same for every refactor, so it is a candidate for a skill. The hazard is that once the rule lives in a skill, you no longer see it, and a colleague using your skill may not know that the whole trust argument rests on it. A skill is also only an instruction; the deny rules and git checks hold whether or not the agent reads it. If you build one, keep the "reference stays with the human" clause as a visible line. An example to compare with your own, stored in `.agents/skills/characterisation-refactor/SKILL.md` as in [Block 5](11e-instructions-skills.qmd): :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Example: `characterisation-refactor/SKILL.md` ```markdown --- name: characterisation-refactor description: >- Refactors working R analysis code into documented functions under a characterisation test, so the output is proved unchanged. Use when asked to functionalise, refactor or tidy a script whose output must not change. Not for fixing bugs or changing results. disable-model-invocation: true --- # Refactor under a characterisation test ## The reference stays with the human The frozen reference in tests/fixtures/ is captured by the user, once, before any refactoring. A reference produced by the code under test proves nothing. - Never create, regenerate or modify anything under tests/fixtures/. - Never run tests/make_reference.R or any script that writes a fixture. - If no reference exists, stop and ask the user to capture one. ## Procedure 1. Present a plan: the code to move, the function name and file, and the test file. Wait for the user to confirm. 2. Refactor only. Write the function in scripts/functions/ with a roxygen2 block and an argument check, and make the original script call it. Do not write or edit tests in this step. Stop and let the user review the diff. 3. Test only. Write a testthat file that reads the reference from tests/fixtures/ and compares it with the function's output using expect_equal(). Never hard-code expected values, and never reimplement the computation inside the test. Include an expect_error() test showing that the argument check rejects data with a required column missing. 4. Run the tests in a fresh R session and report the output verbatim. ## Rules - If the test fails, report the difference. Never change the test, the tolerance or the reference to make it pass. - Sort the output rows explicitly with dplyr::arrange() on the grouping columns, so the order never depends on how the data happen to be stored. - Do not change behaviour, including how missing values are handled. A passing test shows the output is unchanged, not that it is correct; list anything that looks wrong for the user to decide. ``` ::: **Take it home (1 minute).** Save the example so you can use it on your own code. In the R console, `usethis::edit_file(".agents/skills/characterisation-refactor/SKILL.md")` creates and opens the file; paste the text above and save. Then copy it where Claude Code looks: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fs::dir_copy( here::here(".agents", "skills", "characterisation-refactor"), here::here(".claude", "skills", "characterisation-refactor"), overwrite = TRUE ) ``` ::: **You are done when** `.claude/skills/characterisation-refactor/SKILL.md` exists. After restarting Claude Code (`/exit`, then `claude`), typing `/` lists it. :::{.callout-note} ## Check · Reproduce · Record - **You can now:** let an agent refactor working analysis code into a tested function, **trusted because** a reference only you created proves the output is unchanged, and a known-answer test checks any change you decide to make. - **Check:** the reference you captured, read by a test the agent wrote in a separate prompt; the four-point checklist; and a known-answer test, because unchanged is not correct. - **Reproduce:** `renv::status()` and the tests passing in a fresh R session (`callr`), with nothing changed under `tests/fixtures/`. - **Record:** any re-captured reference is a decision with a commit message that says why. Add a line to `docs/ai-log.md`: the two prompts, whether the test passed first time, and what you changed. ::: ## Check your understanding **A characterisation test passes after a refactor. What has it established?**
**Why must the agent never generate the reference file?**
**The shipped deny rules protect tests/fixtures/ in Claude Code. Which action could still change the reference?**

Apply the same four-point checklist from Step 1, and check the Git pane for anything changed under `tests/fixtures/`. :::: ::: ### An asynchronous agent: the Copilot cloud agent The same work can be handed to an agent that runs remotely while you do something else. It works on a branch in GitHub's infrastructure and returns a pull request. Before you start, check that your Copilot plan includes the cloud agent, that `copilot-setup-steps.yml` is on your default branch (see the next section), and that the repository is protected. **Protect the reference on GitHub.** Local deny rules do not exist for a remote agent. Add a `.github/CODEOWNERS` file naming yourself for the protected paths, and turn on branch protection for `main` so that merging requires your review and a passing `r-checks` run: ``` /tests/fixtures/ @your-github-username /tests/make_reference.R @your-github-username /.github/ @your-github-username ``` Keep the two-step discipline by writing **two issues**, and assign the second only after you have reviewed and merged the first. **Issue 1** ```text Title: Move the metabolic-rate summary into a function Move the summary computation in scripts/05_analysis.R into a documented function summarise_metabolic_rate() in scripts/functions/summary_functions.R, with a roxygen2 block and an argument check. Make 05_analysis.R call it. Acceptance criteria: - Do not add or change anything under tests/, data/ or .github/. - The output must be identical to the current output, including row order and the existing NA value. ``` **Issue 2 (after Issue 1 is merged)** ```text Title: Add a characterisation test for summarise_metabolic_rate() Add tests/test_summary_functions.R. It must call local_edition(3), source scripts/functions/load_voles.R and scripts/functions/summary_functions.R, and compare summarise_metabolic_rate(load_voles()) with tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds using expect_equal(). Acceptance criteria: - Do not create, modify or regenerate anything under tests/fixtures/, and do not run tests/make_reference.R. - Run the tests and report the result in the pull request description. ``` Assign each issue to Copilot. When a pull request arrives: 1. Open **Files changed**. Confirm that only the expected files changed. A change under `tests/fixtures/` or `.github/` should not merge, and CODEOWNERS will in any case require your review for it. 2. Read the test against the four-point checklist in Step 1. 3. Check that the `r-checks` run on the pull request passed. 4. Pull the branch and run the test on your own machine. The agent's report that "tests pass" is its claim; your run is the check. If something is wrong, comment on the pull request to ask for a revision, or close it. Nothing reaches `main` until you merge. ### The environment the test runs in A characterisation test is only as stable as the environment it runs in. The column types in `load_voles()` handle the finest-grained part. The R version and the package set are handled by two GitHub Actions workflows. `r-checks.yml` is the independent check. It runs the tests from a clean checkout on every push to `main` and on every pull request: ```yaml name: r-checks on: push: branches: [main] pull_request: jobs: tests: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2 with: r-version: "4.5.2" # match the R version in renv.lock use-public-rspm: true - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@v2 - name: Run tests run: Rscript -e 'testthat::test_dir("tests", stop_on_failure = TRUE)' ``` It is independent of your machine and of the agent's environment, but it is not tamper-proof. A pull request can change the workflow file or the reference it checks against. CODEOWNERS and branch protection (above) are what make a passing run meaningful: you review every change to those paths before it merges. `copilot-setup-steps.yml` builds the environment the Copilot cloud agent works in. Following GitHub's documented pattern: ```yaml name: "Copilot Setup Steps" # Runs when this file changes, so you can see whether setup succeeds, # and can be run by hand from the Actions tab. on: workflow_dispatch: push: paths: - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml pull_request: paths: - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml jobs: # The job must be called copilot-setup-steps or Copilot will not use it. copilot-setup-steps: runs-on: ubuntu-latest permissions: contents: read steps: - name: Check out repository uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Set up R uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2 with: r-version: "4.5.2" # match the R version in renv.lock use-public-rspm: true - name: Restore packages from renv.lock uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@v2 ``` Four requirements, each with a different failure mode: - **The job name must be exactly `copilot-setup-steps`.** If it is not, Copilot ignores the file and works without your packages. That failure is usually loud: the tests error on the first missing function. - **The file must be on the default branch**, or it is not used. - **The runner must be Ubuntu x64 Linux**, the only runner type the cloud agent supports. - **The lockfile must be restored.** If it restores the wrong versions, the failure is quiet: tests run and pass against different package behaviour. The frozen reference then certifies sameness against the wrong baseline. When the agent's test run and the independent `r-checks` run disagree, suspect the environment before you suspect the code. ## Glossary ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
term definition
characterisation test A test that checks new code reproduces the saved output of the original code exactly. It shows the output is unchanged, not that it is correct.
deny rule A permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code's built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files.
fixture A file a test reads as fixed input or expected output. In this course, the reference .rds file in tests/fixtures/.
fresh R session An R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with "never save .RData" set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record.
known-answer test A test that checks code against a result worked out independently, for example by hand. It can show code is correct, where a characterisation test only shows it is unchanged.
lockfile The renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment.
reference In a characterisation test, the saved output of the original, trusted code (stored in tests/fixtures/). You capture it yourself, once, before any refactoring; the agent never creates or regenerates it.
